zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 ([source](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html); [license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)). The diplomatic readings and English notes in this return are scan-based review work, not a reproduction of that index.

lines.note: Kenpu combines silk and cloth, kinu and nuno. The Portuguese begins a description of a kind of fine fabric rather than a modern standardized textile identification.
The gloss specifies fine fabric and a kind of linen cloth. This completes the paired material explanation of kenpu.
Kenpushou begins a contrast between wise, virtuous people and those of lower standing. The circumflex and nasal abbreviation in Homẽs remain as printed.

runs.text: homẽs baixos, ou de baixa ſorte: ou altos, &

lines.note: The other group is described as low or of low rank; the gloss then restates the contrast as high and low. The colon is part of that explanation.
Baixos completes 'high and low'. The final S. is an upright written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kenkei is a promise or agreement made beforehand. Historical concerto means an arrangement here and is not replaced by a modern synonym.
Kenken and kenken to imitate a dog's barking. The alternative retains its nasal abbreviation qenqẽto, rather than spelling out the omitted n.

runs.text: Modo, ou feição de ſerra, ou lugar

lines.note: A separate kenken describes the configuration of a mountain or place. Its steep, rugged character is specified in the continuation.
The terrain is steep and rugged. Kenken to shitaru begins the example, with the false OCR space after Q removed and the printed xi- division retained.
Shitaru yama completes the description of a rugged, steep mountain. The Portuguese corresponds directly to the Japanese example.
Kenken to also means harshly. The example repeats the form with an abbreviation tilde; its Q is not a separate word.
Mono wo yuu completes 'say something harshly'. The source's yǔ caron and the abbreviated Portuguese adverb remain unchanged.
Kenkwa is a quarrel or fight, explained by the noisy quality kamabisushi. The example repeats the headword across the line-end division.
Completes kenka wo suru, to quarrel or fight. The historical qua spelling remains in the canonical text.
Kenkwa kouron denotes a fight or verbal dispute. The Portuguese palavras is divided after pa-.
Lauras completes palauras, words. The u is the source's spelling, not a modernization to v.
Kenkwa toujou is fighting and uproar. The headword is not split after Q; its two different vowel marks are retained.
Kenryo denotes prudent consideration, explained by thinking wisely. The printed vomonbacaru is preserved without imposing a modern omonpakaru spelling.
Kenro is something revealed or known, arawareta koto. The Portuguese definition continues with the quality of being manifest.
The example gives kenro or roken shita, retaining the two orders of the compound. The false OCR space in Qenro is removed; the initial l is an alternative marker.
Koto completes the preceding expressions for something revealed. Idem refers them back to the same known-or-manifest sense.
A separate kenro is a difficult road, kewashii michi. Qeuaxij is one word; the Portuguese adds steepness on the next row.
'Steep' completes the description of the rough road. This is a short Portuguese continuation, not another Japanese entry.
Another kenro denotes a lame donkey, ashi nayetaru roba. The Portuguese specifies disabled feet and divides tolheitos at the edge.
Completes tolheitos, describing the donkey's disabled feet. The final S. is a roman written-usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Kenro na returns to the rough-road sense. The Portuguese says that the road is rough and laborious to traverse, with trabalhoso divided here.
Lhoſo completes trabalhoſo. This continuation belongs to the adjective kenro na.
Kenro ni supplies the corresponding adverb. The source gives only the grammatical label, so no Portuguese gloss is invented.
Kensai is prudence or sagacity. The initial Q belongs to the headword, correcting the OCR's artificial internal separation.
Kensatsu is explained as making a wise inference, kashikoku sassuru. The printed mixed ſs sequence and abbreviated bẽ are preserved rather than regularized.
Go-kensatsu nasarei is a respectful request to judge or infer. The Portuguese imperative conjeiturai is divided after conjei-.
Completes the imperative 'infer well'. This is the continuation of the preceding respectful Japanese example.
Kenso denotes difficult terrain, with repeated kewashii in the Japanese explanation. The repetition is printed and is not removed as an OCR duplication.
Completes serra and compares the place to a steep, difficult mountain. This supplies the terrain sense of kenso.
Kenso na describes a steep place or road. The definition continues its difficult-terrain sense before introducing a figurative human application.
The terrain is difficult or rough. The printed paragraph mark introduces Per met. and the metaphorical application to a person; it is retained in the italic explanatory passage.

runs.text: Homem aſpero, ou de ruim con-

lines.note: Completes kenso na hito, a harsh person or someone of bad disposition. The metaphor transfers the roughness of terrain to character.
Dição completes condição, disposition or character. It belongs to the figurative human sense of the preceding entry.
Kentai is weariness and neglect, explained by umi okotaru. The source's priguiça begins here with pri-, not a modernized pre- spelling.
Completes priguiça, laziness. The final S. is upright and marks the written usage. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Arremeter, ou ir pera dar, & eſpe-

lines.note: A distinct kentai concerns advancing to strike and waiting for a blow. The Portuguese definition begins its second action with divided esperar.

runs.text: rar a pancada. Palaura que ſe vſa na arte de

lines.note: Completes esperar a pancada and identifies the expression as a technical term in an art. The specific discipline is supplied on the next row.
Esgrima identifies fencing as the discipline. This short row completes the technical usage note, not a separate entry.
Kentetsu concerns wise, sound understanding. The Japanese explanatory words and the checked final t are retained without grammatical expansion.
The definition adds penetrating or thoroughly grasping things. It completes the intellectual quality named by kentetsu.
Kentetsu na and kentetsu na hito describe a prudent person. The source attaches na directly after the checked t and divides Portuguese prudente.

runs.text: dente, & que penetra bem as couſas.

lines.note: Completes prudente and describes a person who understands things deeply. This is the final body row in the first column.
Kentou is the strength or heart of winter, its most intense part. The circumflex is retained as printed.
The example describes intense winter cold associated with snow. The scan restores the paragraph mark and full roman Qentô; ſoxetno is retained without supplying an expected long-vowel mark.
Winter and snow complete the description of the cold. The final S. is the upright usage label. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Qenun. Me curumequ. i, Mega mǒ.

lines.note: Kenun is described through me kurumeku and me ga mou, dizziness or darkening vision. The Portuguese doença begins here with a nasal abbreviation and visible division.

runs.text: ça de andar o miollo à roda, ou irſe o lume

lines.note: The source describes the brain seeming to go round or the light departing from one's eyes. These are its descriptive glosses, not a modern diagnostic claim.
'Of the eyes' completes the phrase about losing the light of vision. The line finishes the dizziness entry.
Ken-ou is a wise king, kashikoi ou. The lowercase caxicoi and tightly set Reyſabio are retained, as are both printed carons.
Kensha denotes a wise person, kashikoi mono. The Portuguese definition adds further qualities on the next row.

runs.text: forte, ou constante, & abſoluto em ſuas acçoẽs.

lines.note: The wise person is firm or constant and independent in actions. The nasal mark remains on the printed vowel in acçoẽs.

runs.text: O que vai ver as rẽdas, ou terras pe-

lines.note: A separate kensha is someone sent to inspect revenues or land. The initial Q is not a separate word, and pera is divided after pe-.
Completes pera and states the purpose: determining how much the holding contains or yields. This is the inspector sense of kensha.

Kensei denotes imposing display and power. The provisional st typography in Fausto is retained, while final S. is visibly upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: Qenxei. i, Xeijinno xei, qenjinno qen.

lines.note: This kensei is explained by the sei of seijin and the ken of kenjin. The source explicitly identifies the compound's elements; their stated order is not rearranged.
The first kind of wisdom belongs to a constant, independent person. The following row contrasts a gentler, more accommodating kind.

runs.text: & prudẽcia de homẽ brando q̃ cõtemporiza

lines.note: The second kind belongs to a mild person who accommodates others. The scan reads cõtemporiza, with o after p rather than the OCR e; the nasal abbreviations are retained.
'More with others' completes the description of accommodation. This finishes the contrast within the kensei definition.
Kenseki is explained by seme semuru and saisoku, pressing or urging someone. The Portuguese oprimir begins with a visible line-end division.

runs.text: mir, ou pòr em aperto, ou fazer força, como

lines.note: Completes oprimir and gives alternatives of putting someone under pressure or applying force. The grave-like mark in pòr is preserved; the example follows below.
Making someone pay debts illustrates the pressure or demand. The printed diuidas is preserved with historical u for consonantal v.

runs.text: Qenxi. Sono tocorono cotouo xiru tçucai.

lines.note: Kenshi is an emissary who ascertains a place's affairs. The scan has a complete roman Qenxi, correcting the OCR's italic O and separated enxi.

runs.text: O que he mandado de peßoa nobre pera ver al

lines.note: The emissary is sent by a noble person to inspect a place. Algum is divided without a securely printed hyphen, so none is added.

runs.text: gum lugar, ou terras, ou pera execução, ou re-

lines.note: Completes algum and extends the remit to lands, execution of an order, or reform. Reformação is divided after re-.
Completes reformação and states that some matter is to be put right. The tilde in dalgũa remains on u as printed.
Kenshin is a wise retainer, kashikoi shinka. Vt introduces the maxim about whom such a retainer serves.
Kenshin jikun ni tsukaezu states that a wise retainer does not serve two lords. The printed ji in jicunni is retained rather than changed from the Portuguese meaning.

runs.text: dente não ſerue a dous ſenhores.

lines.note: Completes prudente and gives the maxim's negative statement about serving two masters. The historical dous is preserved.
Kenshu is a wise lord, kashikoi shuu. The headword has no added vowel mark, while the explanatory xǔ visibly has a caron.
Kenyaku is a firm promise, kataki yakusoku. The Portuguese second equivalent follows below, and the visible ß form in Promeßa is retained.
A firm agreement completes this definition of kenyaku. Concerto is the source's word for an arrangement or compact.
A second kenyaku is a promise made beforehand, kanete no yakusoku. Here Promeſſa shows two tall s forms, unlike the preceding entry's ligature-like ß.
The alternative gloss is an agreement made previously. It completes the prior-arrangement sense, distinct from the preceding firmness sense.
Kenyo is praising and extolling, home kakaguru. The Portuguese engrandecer is divided after en-.
Completes engrandecer and begins an example about seeing a lord's single good deed or virtue. Qimino is one word, correcting the OCR's separated Q.
The conditional continues 'when one sees it', followed by doing one's utmost in praise. The historical toqinba and motte are retained, with kenyo divided after qen-.
Yo ſu completes kenyo su. Xix. is the upright citation label, followed by the Portuguese rendering about seeing a virtue or good example.

runs.text: exemplo do ſenhor, todos grãdemente o louuão,

lines.note: The good example belongs to the lord, whom everyone praises greatly. The printed abbreviated grãdemente and historical louuão are preserved.
The observers are encouraged to imitate the good example. The scan's tightly joined animãoao is retained rather than silently separated.
Kenyou combines dog and sheep, inu and hitsuji. Its circumflex distinguishes it graphically from the neighbouring unaccented Qenyo entries.
This kenyo is explained as a matter of beginning, hajime no gi. The Portuguese describes something present from the beginning and divides principio.
Completes principio and adds the alternative 'that began'. The abbreviation q̃ is preserved without expansion.
Kenyo mo nai describes something not even contemplated or possible. The OCR's false break after Q is removed, while the printed attachment of mo is retained.

runs.text: hum fez, ou que não podia ſer, &c.

lines.note: Completes the idea of something a person did not do even in thought, or that could not be. The source gives these alternatives without further contextual specification.

Kenyu is glossed by the anatomical expression 'little bells of the mouth', referring to the uvular structure. The source's plural campainhas is retained rather than replaced by a modern singular term.
Kenzan is a kind of tenmoku ware, as the Japanese Temmocuno taguy explains. The printed mm and the final y in taguy are preserved.
The ware is used for drinking tea. The source's porſolanas and capitalized Cha remain within the italic Portuguese gloss, without modern spelling replacements.
Kenzoku is a family or household. The one-line gloss is complete and independent of the following drinking-custom entry.

runs.text: Vinho que bebem os carpinteiros, ou

lines.note: Kenzui is wine drunk by carpenters or others, with the definition continuing beyond this page. The visible Q tail corrects OCR Cenzui; the isolated bottom-right outros is handled as catchword furniture.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: Two small vertically aligned ink marks near the centre of the lower margin are visible as a copy feature; no legible signature or additional word is inferred from them. The stroke after outros is the vertical column rule, not a letter l.
